name: Community Mobilization: Pooling Machinery and Bargaining for Inputs
objectives: In your village or farmer group, map the community's shared farming needs and rank the top three, after asking at least ten households, including women and young farmers
Given the top shared need, call and run a first meeting that agrees one shared goal and written rules, with an agenda, minutes, a named leader for each task and rules on money, decisions and leaving

Given a need for ploughing, threshing or another machine, write a machinery-sharing or tractor-hire plan, covering hire versus buy, a fair booking schedule, fees, a maintenance fund, the operator and what happens if it breaks

Given members' seed and fertilizer orders, plan a bulk purchase, compare at least three supplier quotes and bargain, with deposits recorded, inputs checked as genuine and registered, and receipts in the group's name

While the group handles money and decisions, keep open records, settle disagreements by the agreed steps and give women and youth a real role, so every member can see where each payment went, and women and youth hold tasks or leadership posts

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Mapping your community's needs
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask at least ten households about their farming problems and rank the top three shared needs.
This lesson builds toward: In your village or farmer group, you will map the community's shared farming needs and rank the top three, after asking at least ten households, including women and young farmers.
People join a group when it solves a problem they feel. So before you call a meeting, find out what your neighbours actually need. Do not assume: the leader may think it is a tractor while most farmers say it is fake seed or the price of fertilizer.
Visit or call at least ten households. Ask the same few questions: What are your main crops or animals? What held back your last harvest? What do you pay for ploughing, seed and fertilizer, and when do you get them? What would you do together with neighbours? Ask women and young farmers too, not only the household head; their problems can be different, such as having no land title to get credit or being served last by the tractor.
Write the answers on one sheet: one row per household, one column per problem. Count how many households named each problem. The top three are your community's shared needs. You can also draw a simple map of the village showing farms, roads, input shops and where a tractor or mill is. A phone can help you count and sort the answers.
Step by step:
- Write four or five simple questions.
- Ask at least ten households, including women and young farmers.
- Record the answers in a table: one row per household.
- Count how many named each problem.
- Rank the top three shared needs.
Words to know:
- Mobilization: bringing people together to act on a shared need.
- Needs map: a simple record of what problems households share and where resources are.
- Household: the people who live and farm together and share food and money.
Try it now: Ask at least ten households in your community your questions. Put the answers in a table, count each problem and write down the top three shared needs.
You can now map your community's farming needs and rank the top three shared problems.

check.q: Why ask households before calling a meeting?
options: To find out what problems people really share
check.why: A group lasts when it solves a need most members feel, not only the leader's idea.

check.q: Who should you include when asking about needs?
options: Women and young farmers as well as household heads
check.why: Women and youth can face different problems, so leaving them out gives a wrong picture.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Calling and running a first meeting
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a first meeting with an agenda that ends with clear tasks and minutes.
This lesson builds toward: Given the top shared need, you will call and run a first meeting that agrees one shared goal and written rules, with an agenda, minutes, a named leader for each task and rules on money, decisions and leaving.
Choose a time and place that suit most people: after farm work, not on market day, at a place women and youth can easily reach, such as a school, church, mosque or under a known tree. Invite people personally, by phone, SMS or word of mouth, and through respected people such as the chief, a religious leader or the extension officer. Tell them the purpose in one sentence: 'Let us talk about getting fertilizer cheaper this season.'
Keep an agenda of four or five items and keep the meeting short: welcome and purpose; what the needs map found; ideas for what to do together; agreeing a first step; who does what and by when. Choose someone to chair and someone to write minutes. Let everyone speak, and ask quiet people directly.
End with decisions, not just talk. Write each task, the person responsible and the date. Read the minutes aloud and agree the next meeting. Example: a group of sorghum farmers in Burkina Faso agreed in their first meeting to collect fertilizer orders within two weeks, with two members, one of them a young woman, collecting the list.
Step by step:
- Pick a time and place that suit most people, including women and youth.
- Invite personally and through respected people, with a one-sentence purpose.
- Prepare a short agenda: purpose, needs found, ideas, first step, tasks.
- Choose a chair and a minute-taker; let everyone speak.
- End with tasks, names and dates; read the minutes aloud.
Words to know:
- Agenda: the list of things a meeting will discuss, in order.
- Minutes: the written record of what a meeting decided and who will do what.
- Chair: the person who leads the meeting and keeps it on time.
Try it now: Write the invitation (one sentence of purpose, time and place) and a five-item agenda for your first meeting. If you can, hold it, and write minutes with at least two tasks, names and dates.
You can now call and run a short first meeting that ends with tasks, names, dates and minutes.

check.q: Which meeting time is usually best for farmers?
options: After farm work, at a place most people can reach
Very early, far from the village
check.why: A convenient time and place lets most members, including women and youth, attend.

check.q: How should a first meeting end?
options: With everyone paying money at once
With tasks, names and dates written in the minutes
check.why: Clear tasks with names and dates turn talk into action.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Shared goals, fair rules and including everyone
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a shared goal and five simple rules your group agrees on.
This lesson builds toward: Given the top shared need, you will call and run a first meeting that agrees one shared goal and written rules, with an agenda, minutes, a named leader for each task and rules on money, decisions and leaving. While the group handles money and decisions, you will keep open records, settle disagreements by the agreed steps and give women and youth a real role, so every member can see where each payment went, and women and youth hold tasks or leadership posts.
A shared goal is specific and has a date: 'By 1 March, buy 200 bags of fertilizer together at a lower price than members pay alone.' or 'This season, every member's field is ploughed within two weeks of the first rains.' A clear goal tells members what success looks like.
Agree simple rules before any money moves: who can join and what they pay; how decisions are made (for example one member, one vote, as cooperatives do); who holds money and how (a group bank or mobile money account with two people to approve payments); what happens if someone does not pay or does not deliver; and how a member can leave and get their money back. Write the rules and read them aloud so members who cannot read also agree.
Make room for women and youth on purpose. Hold meetings at times they can attend, let members join in their own name even without land title, and give them real posts such as treasurer, booking agent or input checker. Groups that include them often have more members, more trust and more skills, such as young members who use phones and mobile money well. When your group is ready to register formally, see Farmer Cooperatives and Getting to Market.
Step by step:
- Write one goal with a number and a date.
- Agree rules on joining, decisions, money, failing to pay or deliver, and leaving.
- Read the rules aloud and record agreement in the minutes.
- Give women and youth real posts and meeting times that suit them.
Words to know:
- Shared goal: one clear result the whole group wants, with a number and a date.
- Signatory: a person allowed to approve payments from the group account.
- Inclusion: making sure everyone, including women and young people, can join, speak and lead.
Official sources:
- International Cooperative Alliance: the cooperative identity, values and principles
Try it now: Write your group's shared goal with a number and a date, and five rules covering joining, decisions, money, failing to pay or deliver, and leaving. Name one post that a woman or young member will hold.
You can now write a clear shared goal and fair rules, and give women and youth a real role in the group.

check.q: Which is the clearest shared goal?
options: By 1 March, buy 200 bags of fertilizer together at a lower price
check.why: A goal with a number and a date shows exactly what success looks like.

check.q: A young woman has no land title but farms her own plot. What should the group's rules allow?
options: She joins only through her husband
She can attend but not vote
She joins in her own name and can hold a post
check.why: Letting women and youth join and lead in their own name builds a bigger, stronger group.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Pooling, buying together and keeping trust

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Pooling for machinery and tractor hire
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a plan for sharing a machine or hiring a tractor service as a group.
This lesson builds toward: Given a need for ploughing, threshing or another machine, you will write a machinery-sharing or tractor-hire plan, covering hire versus buy, a fair booking schedule, fees, a maintenance fund, the operator and what happens if it breaks.
First decide: hire or buy? Buying a tractor costs a great deal and needs fuel, repairs, a trained operator and enough work to keep it busy. For most small groups, hiring a tractor service as a group is the first step: a hire provider will often give better timing or price for many fields close together. FAO supports hire services as a way for smallholders to get machinery. Booking apps and agents, such as Hello Tractor in parts of Nigeria and Kenya, link farmers to tractor owners; check what works in your area. Smaller shared machines, such as a thresher, sheller or mill, can be bought by a group.
Plan the schedule fairly. Ploughing or planting late costs yield, and everyone wants the machine on the same days. Agree the order in advance: by area and route to save fuel and travel, by lottery, or by planting needs, and rotate who goes first each season. Write the schedule and share it. Agree what happens if rain or a breakdown stops work.
Agree fees and costs: what members pay per acre or per hour (example figures only: XOF, KES, NGN or GHS per acre), payment before or on the day, and a separate maintenance fund for a group-owned machine so repairs do not stop the season. Name a trained operator, keep a logbook of hours, fuel, fields served and repairs, and store the machine safely.
Step by step:
- Decide hire or buy, based on cost, skills and how much work there is.
- List members' fields, sizes and the dates they need the machine.
- Agree a fair schedule (by route, lottery or planting need) and rotate first place.
- Set fees, payment timing and a maintenance fund.
- Name the operator and keep a logbook; agree what happens if it breaks.
Words to know:
- Hire service: a provider who brings a tractor or machine and does the work for a fee.
- Maintenance fund: money set aside from fees to pay for repairs and servicing.
- Logbook: a record of a machine's hours, fuel, fields served and repairs.
Official sources:
- FAO: Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization: what FAO does (hire services, support for smallholders)
Try it now: Choose the machine or hire service your group needs. List five members' fields, sizes and dates, then write a booking schedule, the fee per acre, a maintenance fund rule if you own the machine, and what happens if it breaks.
You can now write a fair plan to hire or share a tractor or machine, with schedule, fees and maintenance.

check.q: Why do many small groups hire a tractor service instead of buying one?
options: Tractors cannot be bought in Africa
Buying needs a lot of money, repairs, an operator and enough work
Hire services never come on time
check.why: Owning a tractor brings big costs and needs; group hire can give access without them.

check.q: What is a maintenance fund for?
options: Paying for repairs so the machine keeps working
check.why: Setting aside money for repairs stops breakdowns from ending the season.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Bulk buying, bargaining and avoiding fake inputs
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a bulk purchase of seed or fertilizer, compare three quotes and check the inputs are genuine.
This lesson builds toward: Given members' seed and fertilizer orders, you will plan a bulk purchase, compare at least three supplier quotes and bargain, with deposits recorded, inputs checked as genuine and registered, and receipts in the group's name.
Collect orders first: each member's name, the input, the quantity and the deposit paid, all written in an order book and read back. Add up the total. A large, sure order gives you power to bargain. Ask at least three registered suppliers (agro-dealers, distributors or companies) for a written quote: price per bag, delivery to your village, the date, the brand and variety, and any discount for the full load.
Bargain on more than price: free or cheaper delivery, a delivery date before planting, a free demonstration or training, part payment on delivery, and a receipt in the group's name. Compare quotes on the total cost delivered, not just the bag price. Never hand all the money to one person in cash; pay from the group account against a receipt.
Fake seed, fertilizer and pesticide are a real risk. Buy only from registered dealers. Check seals, labels, batch numbers and dates, and that bags are not torn or re-sewn. In Kenya, certified seed is controlled by KEPHIS; in Nigeria, the National Agricultural Seeds Council (NASC) tells farmers to buy from registered agro-dealers and look for its certification tag; in Ghana, the Plant Protection and Regulatory Services Directorate (PPRSD) regulates seed and fertilizer under the Plants and Fertilizer Act. Pesticides must be on your national register. Keep receipts and a small sample, and report fakes to the national body.
Step by step:
- Collect each member's order and deposit in an order book; read it back.
- Get written quotes from at least three registered suppliers.
- Bargain on price, delivery, date, training and payment terms.
- Compare the total delivered cost and choose; pay from the group account against a receipt.
- On delivery, check seals, labels, batch numbers and certification tags; share out with a receipt per member.
Words to know:
- Bulk buying: buying a large amount together to get a lower price or better terms.
- Quote: a supplier's written price and terms before you buy.
- Agro-dealer: a shop or trader that sells seed, fertilizer and other farm inputs.
- Certified seed: seed checked by the national seed body to be the right variety and quality.
Official sources:
- KEPHIS (Kenya): Seed certification and plant variety protection services
- Voice of Nigeria: National Agricultural Seeds Council (NASC) cautions farmers over fake seeds (buy from registered agro-dealers; certification tag)
- UNEP LEAP: Ghana Plants and Fertilizer Act, 2010 (Act 803): seed and fertilizer registration (PPRSD)
- FAO Pesticide Registration Toolkit: national pesticide registers in Africa
Try it now: Make an order sheet for at least five members (name, input, quantity, deposit). Write the questions you will ask three registered suppliers, and a delivery-day checklist for spotting fake seed or fertilizer.
You can now plan a bulk input purchase, bargain with three suppliers and check that seed and fertilizer are genuine.

check.q: How should you compare supplier quotes?
options: The total cost delivered, plus date, quality and terms
check.why: A low bag price can hide high transport or late delivery; compare the full deal.

check.q: On delivery, some seed bags look re-sewn and have no certification tag. What do you do?
options: Refuse them, keep evidence and report to the seed body
check.why: Re-sewn, untagged bags are signs of fake seed; refuse, keep evidence and report.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping trust: open records and handling conflict
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep open records of pooled money and settle a disagreement using agreed steps.
This lesson builds toward: While the group handles money and decisions, you will keep open records, settle disagreements by the agreed steps and give women and youth a real role, so every member can see where each payment went, and women and youth hold tasks or leadership posts.
Groups rarely fail for lack of ideas; they fail when members stop trusting where the money went. Make every shilling, naira, cedi or franc easy to follow: an order book for deposits, a receipt for every payment in and out, payments from a group account that two people approve, and a machine logbook if you share one.
Make records open. Read the money summary aloud at every meeting: money in, money out, balance, and what was bought for whom. Post the order list and schedule where members can see them, or share a photo in the group chat. Let any member look at the books. Change who handles money from time to time.
Disagreements will happen: someone gets the tractor late, a bag is missing, a member does not pay. Use the steps in your rules: first talk directly; then the committee hears both sides and checks the records; then the whole group decides; and if needed, ask a respected outsider such as the extension officer, chief or a cooperative officer. Decide on the facts in the records, not on who is louder. Make sure women and youth can raise problems too, and that their complaints are heard.
Step by step:
- Keep an order book, receipts, a group account with two approvers and a logbook.
- Read the money summary aloud at every meeting.
- Post lists and schedules where members can see them.
- Settle disagreements by the agreed steps, using the records.
- Rotate money posts and make sure everyone can raise a problem.
Words to know:
- Transparency: keeping money and decisions open so every member can see them.
- Mediator: a respected, neutral person who helps two sides settle a disagreement.
- Balance: the money left after money out is taken from money in.
Try it now: Final task: write your bulk-input purchase plan or machinery-sharing agreement. Include the members, the records you will keep and read aloud, the steps for settling disagreements, and the posts women and youth will hold.
You can now keep pooled money open and traceable, settle disagreements fairly and keep everyone's trust.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Needs map The need is the leader's guess, or fewer than ten households were asked. At least ten households asked, including women and youth, with the top three needs ranked. Includes a simple village map of farms, roads, input shops and machines. Goal and rules No clear goal, or no written rules on money and leaving. A goal with a number and a date, and written rules on joining, decisions, money, failing to pay and leaving, agreed in the minutes. Rules were read aloud and members' agreement is recorded by name. Machinery plan No schedule or fees, or no plan if the machine breaks. Hire or buy decided, a fair schedule, fees, a maintenance fund or hire terms, an operator and a breakdown rule. A hire provider or machine owner has confirmed the plan, and first place rotates by season. Bulk purchase plan No order book, fewer than three quotes, or no check for fake inputs. Orders and deposits recorded, three written quotes compared on delivered cost, payment by group account and a delivery-day check for genuine inputs. Shows what was won in bargaining (price, delivery, training) and names the body to report fakes to. Trust and inclusion Records are kept by one person only, or women and youth have no role. Open records read aloud, agreed steps for disagreements, and named posts for women and youth. Money posts rotate, and women and youth hold at least one leadership post. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and try again.

check.q: What builds the most trust in a group that pools money?
options: The treasurer keeps the books at home
Reading money in, out and balance aloud at every meeting
Paying suppliers in cash with no receipt
Only the chair knows the balance
check.why: Open records let every member see where the money went.

check.q: A member says she got the tractor last again. What is the first step?
options: Talk directly, then check the schedule and records
Give her money back and close the group
check.why: Following the agreed steps and checking the records settles it fairly.
